L24: # GetTickCount64 function (sysinfoapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Retrieves the number of milliseconds that have elapsed since the system was started.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `ULONGLONG GetTickCount64();
L37:     `
L38: 
L39: ## Return value
L40: 
L41: The number of milliseconds.
L42: ## Remarks
L43: 
L44: The resolution of the GetTickCount64 function is limited to the resolution of the system timer, which is typically in the range of 10 milliseconds to 16 milliseconds. The resolution of the GetTickCount64 function is not affected by adjustments made by the cite5†GetSystemTimeAdjustment function.
L45: 
L46: If you need a higher resolution timer, use a cite6†multimedia timer or a cite7†high-resolution timer .
L47: To obtain the time the system has spent in the working state since it was started, use the cite8†QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime function.
L48: 
L49: Note  The cite8†QueryUnbiasedInterruptTime function produces different results on debug ("checked") builds of Windows, because the interrupt-time count and tick count are advanced by approximately 49 days. This helps to identify bugs that might not occur until the system has been running for a long time.
L50: To compile an application that uses this function, define _WIN32_WINNT as 0x0600 or later. For more information, see cite9†Using the Windows Headers .

L24: # ExitWindowsEx function (winuser.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Logs off the interactive user, shuts down the system, or shuts down and restarts the system. It sends the cite5†WM_QUERYENDSESSION message to all applications to determine if they can be terminated.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `BOOL ExitWindowsEx(
L37:       [in] UINT  uFlags,
L38:       [in] DWORD dwReason
L39:     );
L40:     `
L41: ## Parameters
L42: 
L43: `[in] uFlags`
L44: 
L45: The shutdown type. This parameter must include one of the following values.
L46: 
L47: Value  | Meaning
L48: --- | ---
L49: 
L50: EWX_HYBRID_SHUTDOWN
L51: 0x00400000
L52:  | Beginning with Windows 8:  You can prepare the system for a faster startup by combining the EWX_HYBRID_SHUTDOWN flag with the EWX_SHUTDOWN flag.
L53: EWX_LOGOFF
L54: 0
L55:  | Shuts down all processes running in the logon session of the process that called the ExitWindowsEx function. Then it logs the user off. This flag can be used only by processes running in an interactive user's logon session.
L56: 
L57: EWX_POWEROFF
L58: 0x00000008
L59:  | Shuts down the system and turns off the power. The system must support the power-off feature. The calling process must have the SE_SHUTDOWN_NAME privilege. For more information, see the following Remarks section.
L60: EWX_REBOOT
L61: 0x00000002
L62:  | Shuts down the system and then restarts the system. The calling process must have the SE_SHUTDOWN_NAME privilege. For more information, see the following Remarks section.
L63: EWX_RESTARTAPPS
L64: 0x00000040
L65:  | Shuts down the system and then restarts it, as well as any applications that have been registered for restart using the cite6†RegisterApplicationRestart function. These application receive the cite5†WM_QUERYENDSESSION message with lParam set to the ENDSESSION_CLOSEAPP value. For more information, see cite7†Guidelines for Applications .
L66: EWX_SHUTDOWN
L67: 0x00000001
L68:  | Shuts down the system to a point at which it is safe to turn off the power. All file buffers have been flushed to disk, and all running processes have stopped. The calling process must have the SE_SHUTDOWN_NAME privilege. For more information, see the following Remarks section. Specifying this flag will not turn off the power even if the system supports the power-off feature.
L69: You must specify EWX_POWEROFF to do this.Windows XP with SP1:  If the system supports the power-off feature, specifying this flag turns off the power.
L70: This parameter can optionally include one of the following values.
L71: 
L72: Value  | Meaning
L73: --- | ---
L74: 
L75: EWX_FORCE
L76: 0x00000004
L77:  | This flag has no effect if terminal services is enabled. Otherwise, the system does not send the cite5†WM_QUERYENDSESSION message. This can cause applications to lose data. Therefore, you should only use this flag in an emergency.
L78: EWX_FORCEIFHUNG
L79: 0x00000010
L80:  | Forces processes to terminate if they do not respond to the cite5†WM_QUERYENDSESSION or cite8†WM_ENDSESSION message within the timeout interval. For more information, see the Remarks.
L81: 
L82: `[in] dwReason`
L83: 
L84: The reason for initiating the shutdown. This parameter must be one of the cite9†system shutdown reason codes .
L85: If this parameter is zero, the SHTDN_REASON_FLAG_PLANNED reason code will not be set and therefore the default action is an undefined shutdown that is logged as "No title for this reason could be found". By default, it is also an unplanned shutdown. Depending on how the system is configured, an unplanned shutdown triggers the creation of a file that contains the system state information, which can delay shutdown. Therefore, do not use zero for this parameter.
L86: ## Return value
L87: 
L88: If the function succeeds, the return value is nonzero. Because the function executes asynchronously, a nonzero return value indicates that the shutdown has been initiated. It does not indicate whether the shutdown will succeed. It is possible that the system, the user, or another application will abort the shutdown.
L89: 
L90: If the function fails, the return value is zero. To get extended error information, call cite10†GetLastError .
L91: ## Remarks
L92: 
L93: The ExitWindowsEx function returns as soon as it has initiated the shutdown process. The shutdown or logoff then proceeds asynchronously. The function is designed to stop all processes in the caller's logon session. Therefore, if you are not the interactive user, the function can succeed without actually shutting down the computer. If you are not the interactive user, use the cite11†InitiateSystemShutdown or cite12†InitiateSystemShutdownEx function.
L94: A non-zero return value does not mean the logoff was or will be successful. The shutdown is an asynchronous process, and it can occur long after the API call has returned, or not at all. Even if the timeout value is zero, the shutdown can still be aborted by applications, services, or even the system. The non-zero return value indicates that the validation of the rights and parameters was successful and that the system accepted the shutdown request.
L95: When this function is called, the caller must specify whether or not applications with unsaved changes should be forcibly closed. If the caller chooses not to force these applications to close and an application with unsaved changes is running on the console session, the shutdown will remain in progress until the user logged into the console session aborts the shutdown, saves changes, closes the application, or forces the application to close.
L96: During this period, the shutdown may not be aborted except by the console user, and another shutdown may not be initiated.
L97: Calling this function with the value of the uFlags parameter set to EWX_FORCE avoids this situation. Remember that doing this may result in loss of data.
L98: 
L99: To set a shutdown priority for an application relative to other applications in the system, use the cite13†SetProcessShutdownParameters function.
L100: During a shutdown or log-off operation, running applications are allowed a specific amount of time to respond to the shutdown request. If this time expires before all applications have stopped, the system displays a user interface that allows the user to forcibly shut down the system or to cancel the shutdown request. If the EWX_FORCE value is specified, the system forces running applications to stop when the time expires.
L101: If the EWX_FORCEIFHUNG value is specified, the system forces hung applications to close and does not display the dialog box.
L102: Console processes receive a separate notification message, CTRL_SHUTDOWN_EVENT or CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT, as the situation warrants. A console process routes these messages to its cite14†HandlerRoutine function. ExitWindowsEx sends these notification messages asynchronously; thus, an application cannot assume that the console notification messages have been handled when a call to ExitWindowsEx returns.
L103: To shut down or restart the system, the calling process must use the cite15†AdjustTokenPrivileges function to enable the SE_SHUTDOWN_NAME privilege. For more information, see cite16†Running with Special Privileges .
L104: #### Examples
L105: 
L106: For an example, see cite17†How to Shut Down the System .

L24: # OpenProcess function (processthreadsapi.h)
L25: 
L26: Feedback
L27: 
L28: Summarize this article for me
L29: 
L30: ## In this article
L31: 
L32: Opens an existing local process object.
L33: 
L34: ## Syntax
L35: 
L36:     `HANDLE OpenProcess(
L37:       [in] DWORD dwDesiredAccess,
L38:       [in] BOOL  bInheritHandle,
L39:       [in] DWORD dwProcessId
L40:     );
L41:     `
L42: ## Parameters
L43: 
L44: `[in] dwDesiredAccess`
L45: 
L46: The access to the process object. This access right is checked against the security descriptor for the process. This parameter can be one or more of the cite5†process access rights .
L47: 
L48: If the caller has enabled the cite6†SeDebugPrivilege privilege , the requested access is granted regardless of the contents of the security descriptor.
L49: 
L50: `[in] bInheritHandle`
L51: If this value is TRUE, processes created by this process will inherit the handle. Otherwise, the processes do not inherit this handle.
L52: 
L53: `[in] dwProcessId`
L54: 
L55: The identifier of the local process to be opened.
L56: If the specified process is the System Idle Process (0x00000000), the function fails and the last error code is `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER`. If the specified process is the System process or one of the Client Server Run-Time Subsystem (CSRSS) processes, this function fails and the last error code is `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` because their access restrictions prevent user-level code from opening them.
L57: If you are using cite7†GetCurrentProcessId as an argument to this function, consider using cite8†GetCurrentProcess instead of OpenProcess, for improved performance.
L58: ## Return value
L59: 
L60: If the function succeeds, the return value is an open handle to the specified process.
L61: 
L62: If the function fails, the return value is NULL. To get extended error information, call cite9†GetLastError .
L63: ## Remarks
L64: 
L65: To open a handle to another local process and obtain full access rights, you must enable the SeDebugPrivilege privilege. For more information, see cite10†Changing Privileges in a Token .
L66: 
L67: The handle returned by the OpenProcess function can be used in any function that requires a handle to a process, such as the cite11†wait functions , provided the appropriate access rights were requested.
L68: 
L69: When you are finished with the handle, be sure to close it using the cite12†CloseHandle function.
L70: #### Examples
L71: 
L72: For an example, see cite13†Taking a Snapshot and Viewing Processes .

citeturn14view3 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/power/system-power-states","lineno":125}); Total lines: 194
L57: ## Sleep state: Modern Standby
L58: 
L59: In the S0 low-power idle mode of the working state, also referred to as cite5†Modern Standby , the system remains partially running. During Modern Standby, the system can stay up-to-date whenever a suitable network is available and also wake when real-time action is required, such as OS maintenance. Modern Standby wakes significantly faster than S1-S3. For more info, see cite5†Modern Standby .
L60: 
L61: Note
L62: Modern Standby is only available on some SoC systems. When it's supported, the system doesn't support S1-S3.
L63: 
L64: Caution
L65: 
L66: Do not enable S3 wake-on-LAN (WoL) on Modern Standaby capable systems. Waking a computer with a magic packet is natively supported by Modern Standby. Enabling legacy S3 WoL is not necessary and may cause DHCP and/or DNS packet storms on your network.
L67: ## Sleep state: S1-S3
L68: 
L69: The system enters sleep based on a number of criteria, including user or application activity and preferences that the user sets on the Power & sleep page of Windows Settings. By default, the system uses the lowest-powered sleep state supported by all enabled wake-up devices. For more information about how the system determines when to enter sleep, see cite7†System sleep criteria .
L70: Before the system enters sleep, it determines the appropriate sleep state, notifies applications and drivers of the pending transition, and then transitions the system to the sleep state. In the case of a critical transition, such as when the critical battery threshold is reached, the system doesn't notify applications and drivers. Applications need to be prepared for this and take the appropriate action when the system returns to the working state.
L71: In S1-S3 states, volatile memory is kept refreshed to maintain the system state. Some components remain powered so the computer can wake from input from the keyboard, LAN, or a USB device.
L72: The system also wakes from sleep in response to user activity or a wake-up event defined by an application. For more information, see cite8†System wake-up events . The amount of time it takes the system to wake depends on the sleep state it's waking from. The system takes more time to wake from a lower-powered state (S3) than from a higher-powered state (S1) because of the extra work the hardware may have to do. For example, stabilizing the power supply or re-initializing the processor.
L73: 
L74: Caution
L75: When calling cite9†SetThreadExecutionState , the `ES_AWAYMODE_REQUIRED` value should be used only when absolutely necessary by media applications that require the system to perform background tasks, such as recording television content or streaming media to other devices while the system appears to be sleeping. Applications that don't require critical background processing or that run on portable computers shouldn't enable away mode because it prevents the system from conserving power by entering true sleep.
L76: ### Hybrid sleep: S1-S3 + hibernation file
L77: 
L78: Hybrid sleep is a special state that's a combination of the sleep and hibernation states. It's when a system uses a hibernation file with S1-S3. Hybrid sleep is only available on some systems. When enabled, the system writes a hibernation file but enters a higher-powered sleep state. If power is lost while the system is sleeping, the system wakes from hibernation, which takes longer but restores the user's system state.
L79: ## Hibernate state: S4
L80: Windows uses hibernation to provide a fast startup experience. When available, it's also used on mobile devices to extend the usable battery life of a system by giving a mechanism to save all of the user's state prior to shutting down the system. In a hibernate transition, all the contents of memory are written to a file on the primary system drive, the hibernation file. This preserves the state of the operating system, applications, and devices.
L81: In the case where the combined memory footprint consumes all of physical memory, the hibernation file must be large enough to ensure there's space to save all the contents of physical memory. Since data is written to non-volatile storage, DRAM does not need to maintain self-refresh and can be powered off, which means power consumption of hibernation is very low, almost the same as power off.
L82: During a full shutdown and boot (S5), the entire user session is torn down and restarted on the next boot. In contrast, during a hibernation (S4), the user session is closed and the user state is saved.
L83: ### Fast startup: reduced hibernation file
L84: 
L85: Fast startup is a type of shutdown that uses a hibernation file to speed up the subsequent boot. During this type of shutdown, the user is logged off before the hibernation file is created. Fast startup allows for a smaller hibernation file, more appropriate for systems with less storage capabilities. For more info, see cite10†Hibernation file types .
L86: When using fast startup, the system appears to the user as though a full shutdown (S5) has occurred, even though the system has actually gone through S4. This includes how the system responds to device wake alarms.
L87: 
L88: Fast startup logs off user sessions, but the contents of kernel (session 0) are written to hard disk. This enables faster boot.
L89: To programmatically initiate a fast startup-style shutdown, call the cite11†InitiateShutdown function with the `SHUTDOWN_HYBRID` flag or the cite12†ExitWindowsEx function with the `EWX_HYBRID_SHUTDOWN` flag.
L90: 
L91: Note
L92: 
L93: In Windows, fast startup is the default transition when a system shutdown is requested. A full shutdown (S5) occurs when a system restart is requested or when an application calls a shutdown API.
L94: ### Entering hibernation
L95: 
L96: When a hibernate request is made, the following steps occur as the system enters hibernation:
L97: 
L98:   1. Apps and services are notified
L99:   2. Drivers are notified
L100:   3. User and system state is saved to disk in a compressed format
L101:   4. Firmware is notified
L102: 
L103: Note
L104: 
L105: All cores on the system are used to compress the data in memory and write it to disk.
L106: 
L107: To programmatically initiate a hibernate transition, call the cite13†SetSuspendState function.
L108: ### Resuming from hibernation
L109: 
L110: When a system resumes from hibernation.
L111: 
L112: When a system is powered on, the following steps occur as the system resumes from hibernation:
L113: 
L114:   1. System POST
L115:   2. System memory is decompressed and restored from the hibernation file
L116:   3. Device initialization
L117:   4. Drivers are restored to the state they were in prior to hibernation
L118:   5. Services are restored to the state they were in prior to hibernation
L119:   6. System becomes available for login
L120: A resume from hibernation starts with a system POST that's similar to an S5 shutdown. The OS boot manager determines that a resume from hibernation is required by detecting a valid hibernation file. Then it directs the system to resume, restoring the contents of memory and all architectural registers.
L121: In the case of a resume from hibernation, the contents of the system memory are read back in from the disk, decompressed, and restored, which puts the system in the exact state it was in when it was hibernated. After memory is restored, the devices are re-started, the machine returns to a running state, ready for login.
L122: Note
L123: 
L124: During a resume from hibernation, drivers and services are notified but aren't restarted. They're only restored to the state they were in prior to hibernation.
L125: ### Hibernation file types
L126: 
L127: Hibernation files are used for hybrid sleep, fast startup, and cite14†standard hibernation . There are two types, differentiated by size, a full and reduced size hibernation file. Only fast startup can use a reduced hibernation file.
L128: 
L129: Hibernation file type  | Default size  | Supports...
L130: --- | --- | ---
L131: Full  | 40% of physical memory  | hibernate, hybrid sleep, fast startup
L132: Reduced  | 20% of physical memory  | fast startup
L133: To verify or change the type of hibernation file used, run the powercfg.exe utility. The following examples demonstrate how. For more information, run `powercfg /? hibernate`.
L134: Example  | Description
L135: --- | ---
L136: `powercfg /a`  | Verify the hibernation file type. When a full hibernation file is used, the results state that hibernation is an available option. When a reduced hibernation file is used, the results say hibernation is not supported. If the system has no hibernation file at all, the results say hibernation hasn't been enabled.
L137: `powercfg /h /type full`  | Change the hibernation file type to full. This isn't recommended on systems with less than 32GB of storage.
L138: `powercfg /h /type reduced`  | Change the hibernation file type to reduced. If the command returns "the parameter is incorrect," see the following example.
L139: `powercfg /h /size 0`
L140: `powercfg /h /type reduced`  | Retry changing the hibernation file type to reduced. If the hibernation file is set to a custom size greater than 40%, you must first set the size of the file to zero. Then retry the reduced configuration.
L141: ## Soft off state: S5
L142: 
L143: The soft off state is when the system fully shuts down without a hibernation file. Soft off is also known as a full shutdown. During a full shutdown and boot, the entire user session is torn down and restarted on the next boot. Consequently, a boot/startup from this state takes significantly longer than S1-S4. A full shutdown (S5) occurs when a system restart is requested or when an application calls a shutdown API.
L144: ## Mechanical off state: G3
L145: 
L146: In this state, the system is completely off and consumes no power. The system returns to the working state only after a full reboot.
L147: ## Wake-on-LAN behavior
L148: 
L149: The wake-on-LAN (WOL) feature wakes the computer from a low power state when a network adapter detects a WOL event (typically, a specially constructed Ethernet packet).
L150: 
L151: WOL is supported from S3 sleep or S4 hibernate. It's not supported from fast startup or S5 soft off shutdown states. NICs aren't armed for wake in these states because users don't expect their systems to wake up on their own.
L152: 
L153: Note
L154: WOL is not officially supported from the S5 soft off state. However, the BIOS on some systems might support arming NICs for wake, even though Windows isn't involved in the process.
